SpaceX Jumps 10% as Lockup Fears Ease
data.description:
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX, Financials), Elon Musk's space and AI company, jumped more than 10% as investors grew more comfortable with the stock after its first major post-IPO lockup expiration.

Shares had already gained 6% Thursday even as the number of shares available for trading more than doubled. That matters because investors had worried the sudden increase in supply could trigger another sharp selloff. Instead, the stock held up and extended its rebound Friday.

SpaceX is still trading below its $135 IPO price after a volatile stretch that erased hundreds of billions of dollars in market value.

The risk is not gone. Another 7% of shares are scheduled to unlock on Aug. 21, and the tradable float is expected to keep rising through December.

Investors also remain focused on heavy AI spending and the company's lack of profitability. For now, though, the market appears to be treating the first unlock as less damaging than feared.

Lilly and Novo Win a Key GLP-1 Antitrust Fight
data.description:
Eli Lilly and Co. (LLY, Financials), the drugmaker behind Zepbound, won a legal victory alongside Novo Nordisk after a federal judge dismissed an antitrust lawsuit over access to compounded GLP-1 drugs.

Compounding pharmacy Strive Specialties had argued that Lilly and Novo used exclusive telehealth partnerships to make it harder for doctors to prescribe customized alternatives to their branded treatments.

Judge Micaela Alvarez rejected the claim, finding that Strive had not shown the kind of antitrust injury needed to proceed because compounded products do not compete in the same market as Zepbound and Wegovy.

For Lilly and Novo, the ruling removes one challenge to how they distribute some of the most valuable drugs in the pharmaceutical industry.

The fight is not necessarily over. Strive said it is considering an appeal. Investors will continue watching legal battles around compounded GLP-1 drugs as demand for weight-loss treatments keeps expanding.

data.title: Meta Ruling Could Become a Blueprint for More Child-Safety Suits
data.description:
Meta Platforms slipped 0.21% intraday after a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay an additional $567 million and strengthen child-safety features on its apps. The order brings total penalties in the case to $942 million, following a $375 million jury award in March. The muted stock reaction could reflect how small the sum is against Meta's roughly $1.5 trillion value, though the ruling could open the door to similar suits.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid found Meta to be a "public nuisance," ruling that its platforms are a significant contributor to a youth mental-health crisis in the state. The case accused Meta of exposing children to harmful content. About $420 million of the penalty will fund treatment programs, and the ruling requires Meta to police accounts held by children under 13 and to bar minors from romantic or sexualized interactions with its AI chatbots.

Attorney General Raul Torrez called the ruling "a blueprint." Meta said it disagreed and would appeal. A separate case in Los Angeles found Meta and Alphabet (GOOGL) liable in March.
